A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SceneOrchestra, with matching authors, architecture, training framework, and experiments. All 22 pages of v1 and 26 pages of v2, including supplementary material, are readable and support comparison of text, equations, tables, and figures.

before.justification: V1 reports original scene-generation evaluations, runtime measurements, training and orchestrator ablations, and an 18-participant pairwise user study.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds human ratings, human–judge agreement measurements, and comparisons using stronger orchestrator models.

M1.justification: The two Qwen3-based components, four-stage SFT/DPO curriculum, interleaved discriminator training and distillation, and full-trajectory inference remain unchanged. V2 newly mentions LoRA, but v1 does not specify an alternative fine-tuning implementation; this disclosure does not establish a method change.

E1.justification: The indoor scene-synthesis task, ten template-prompt room types, and complex-instruction scenario remain. V2 replaces ten complex prompts with 70 prompts described as involving unseen room types, but does not identify that set. The changed sample size and seen/unseen composition are clear; whether additional room types or task requirements are covered cannot be established.

E2.justification: Table 5 replaces GPT-5.1 with GPT-5.5 and adds Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview, retaining untuned Qwen3. New Table 9 additionally compares against SceneWeaver equipped with GPT-5.5 or Gemini for stepwise orchestration. These substantially expand the orchestration comparators, while LayoutGPT, Holodeck, I-Design, and original SceneWeaver remain in the main comparison.

E3.justification: The complex-instruction evaluation changes from ten prompts covering four seen and six unseen room types to 70 all-unseen prompts. V2 adds a 16-participant study rating 30 sampled scenes on four 1–10 scales and a controlled SceneWeaver orchestrator-replacement experiment. Section 4.1 also changes the reported visual judge from GPT-4 to GPT-4.1; this establishes a reporting revision, without establishing whether earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a controlled test of whether stronger off-the-shelf SceneWeaver orchestrators explain the gains (Table 9), strengthens the in-context orchestration ablation (Table 5), and tests evaluator validity through human ratings and ranking agreement (Tables 6 and 8). The original training-component ablations and qualitative examples remain. The per-room runtime breakdown is relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V2 introduces Kendall's tau estimation for user–user and user–GPT-4.1 agreement in Table 8. Both versions retain five generations per template prompt and three per complex prompt. Neither reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed-level variability.

E6.justification: Existing results are substantially revised: Table 1 reports average object count 35.2 versus 31.1 and functionality 9.3 versus 9.1; average runtime changes from 27.7 to 39.7 minutes. Baseline cells and training-ablation scores also change. These are reported-value revisions, not established same-setting performance losses. Table 3 uses a different prompt set, and v2 adds human-rating, agreement, stronger-model, and runtime results. The original pairwise preference percentages remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–4, the SFT/DPO objectives, quality and composition scores, and trajectory-selection inequalities remain mathematically unchanged. The implementation paragraph's correction from beta to lambda does not alter Equation 3. No new theorem, proof, or derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: V1's contribution statement claims a 70% synthesis-time reduction, and its conclusion claims using only 30% of the execution time. V2 removes these numerical claims, also omitting runtime from the abstract's closing results sentence, while retaining qualitative efficiency claims elsewhere. The framework, training contributions, and scene-quality claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds a specific limitation: the inherited constrained layout solver may fail to converge in crowded scenes, producing invalid layouts (Section 13). It also interprets the new orchestrator controls as supporting trainable orchestration and the agreement analysis as supporting evaluator validity. Existing hallucination and underlying-tool limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds LoRA disclosure, geometry-based physical-scoring clarification, and study consent/IRB documentation, and corrects the composition-weight label to lambda=0.1. However, it removes the S1/S2/S3 instruction counts and all six reported stage-specific training sample counts. Thresholds and the single interleaved cycle remain in Section 10. The old labeled prompt table disappears; its texts survive in Figures 4 and 6, but the replacement 70-prompt set is not listed.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for LoRA, Ouyang et al.'s instruction-following work, GPT-4.1, GPT-5.5, and Gemini, while removing Gorilla and the generic OpenAI API reference. The reinforcement-learning discussion is refined, and the distinction from SceneSmith/SAGE explicitly mentions global planning. The broader research positioning remains unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 corrects typos and grammar, revises portions of the related-work and experimental descriptions, adds a main-text user-study subsection and acknowledgements, and reorganizes supplementary sections and implementation details. The main narrative and most methodological prose remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands and reorganizes the displays: new Tables 6, 8, and 9 and Figures 8–10; removal of the old prompt table; runtime columns added to Tables 3 and 5; and the former runtime table split into a compact main-text average and an appendix breakdown. Existing qualitative figures are retained, with relocation and limited caption changes.

improvement.justification: The added human ratings and agreement analysis, together with stronger orchestrator controls, provide better support for the quality and orchestration claims than v1's existing comparisons alone. Withdrawing the numerical speedup claim and stating the crowded-scene failure condition improve qualification of the conclusions. These gains are tempered by removal of training-size disclosures and inadequate specification of the replacement 70-prompt test set, yielding a limited overall improvement.
